source_text: In Zacchaeum Ἀμφιλοχίου ἐπισκόπου Ἰκονίου λόγος εἰς τὸν Ζακχαῖον. Οὐδὲν οὕτως τὴν ψυχὴν πρὸς εὐφροσύνην διανίστησιν ὡς φόβος θεοῦ καὶ κακῶν ἀποχὴ καὶ μετανοίας δρόμος καὶ ἐξομο λογήσεως τρόπος. Ὅθεν καὶ σήμερον ∆αβὶδ τοὺς τῆς ἀφέσεως τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τυχόντας ἐμακάριζεν ἅμα μὲν τὴν φιλανθρωπίαν τοῦ Χριστοῦ παριστῶν, ἅμα δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς προσδραμεῖν τῇ μετανοίᾳ παρασκευάζων ... μακάριοι, φησίν, ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ... τις οὖνη πόρνοςτελώνης εἰς τὰς ἀκενώτους τῆς σωτη ρίας τοῦ Χριστοῦ τρεχέτωπηγάς. Οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ αὐτῆς οὐ κακῶν λύσιν λαβεῖν οὐ τοῦ μακαρισμοῦ τυχεῖν, κἂν προφήτας κἂν ἀποστόλους κἂν εὐαγγελιστὰς εἴπῃς. Πάντες γὰρ ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ἤντλησαν πηγῆς. Ἐν προφήταις μὲν αὐτὸς ὁ ∆αβὶδ μετὰ μοιχείαν ἔτι καὶ νῦν προφήτης ὢν διὰ τὴν τοῦ συγχωρήσαντος χάριν. Ἐν ἀποστόλοις δὲ Πέτρος καὶ Παῦλος, ὁ μὲν γὰρ μετὰ τὴν ἄρνησιν τὰς κλεῖς τῆς βασιλείας ἔχει, ὁ δὲ μετὰ τὴν δίωξιν τῶν ἐθνῶν κατέστη ἀπόστολος τὸν Ἰουδαϊκὸν ζῆλον εἰς εὐαγγελικὸν μετα θεὶς τρόπον. Ἐν γὰρ τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις οὐ Ματθαῖον μόνον σῳζόμενον ἐκ τελωνῶν οἶδα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑτέρους σὺν αὐτῷ δύο· ὧν εἷς μὲν προσευχόμενος ἐκ τοῦ τὸ στῆθος τύπτειν, τὸν θησαυρὸν τῶν κακῶν, ἐκ τοῦ μὴ τολμᾶν ἐπᾶραι τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὰ ἅγια, ἐκ τοῦ κάτω νεύειν οὐ μόνον ἐδικαιώθη, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ φαρισαῖον ἐστεφανώθη· Ζακχαῖος δὲ ἀνελθὼν ἐπὶ τὸ δένδρον ἐν ᾧ πολλά κις ἑστὼς κατεσκόπει μὴ πού τις τῶν ἐμπόρων λαθὼν παρέλθῃ ὅπως μὴ ἀζήμιος μείνῃ, ἐτήρει μὴ λάθῃ αὐτὸν παραδραμὼν ὁ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς ἔμπορος, ὁ τὸν ἄσυλον τῆς βασιλείας ἐπιφερό μενος θησαυρόν.Ἵνα δὲ μὴ ὅλως ὁμοῦ τῶν τελωνῶν συγχέωμεν τὰς ἱστορίας, εἰ δοκεῖ, σήμερον τὸν Ζακχαῖον μόνον λαβόντες εἰς ὑπόθεσιν πραγματείας τὸν λόγον εὐρύνωμεν. Ἐξελθών, φησίν, ὁ Ἰησοῦς διήρχετο τὴν Ἰεριχὼ καὶ ἰδοὺ ἀνὴρ ὀνόματι καλούμενος Ζακχαῖος καὶ οὗτος ἦν ἀρχιτελώνης. Οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ τῆς Ἰεριχὼ μέμνηται ὁ εὐαγγελιστής, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ τελώνην οἴκοι φιλοφρονησάμενον θεὸν λέγει. Ἄπιστον δὲ ἦν τὸ πρᾶγμα. Προτίθησιν αὐτοῦ τὴν πατρί δα, ἵνα τῆς πόρνης ὑπομνησθέντες Ῥαὰβ μὴ ξενισθῶμεν πρὸς τὴν ξένην Ζακχαίου παλινοδίαν. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο οὖν ἐμνήσθη τῆς Ἰεριχώ, ἵνα ἐν νῷ λαβόντες Ῥαὰβ τὴν πόρνην συγκρίνωμεν ἀμφοτέρων τῆς σωτηρίας τὸν τρόπον. Ὥσπερ γὰρ Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη Ἰησοῦν τὸν τοῦ Ναυὴ ὡς κατάσκοπον δεξαμένη ἔκρυψεν, οὕτω καὶ Ζακχαῖος ὁ τελώνης τὸν ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν τὸν κατασκο πεύοντα ἡμῶν τὴν διάνοιαν οἴκοι δεξάμενος ἔθρεψεν. Ἐκείνη Ἰησοῦν τὸν τοῦ Ναυὴ ἐδέξατο τὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τὸν λαὸν εἰσαγαγόντα· οὗτος τὸν ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν δέχεται τὸν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶ κατ . Ἐκείνη Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν lacuna septem linearum οὗτος τὸν ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐδαφίσαντα ναόν· Οὐ μὴ γάρ, φησί, μείνῃ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον ὃς οὐ μὴ καταλυθήσεται. Ἐκείνη Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν διὰ τοῦ Ἰορδάνουτὸν λαὸν εἰς γῆν ῥέουσαν γάλα καὶ μέλι εἰσαγαγόντα· οὗτος τὸν ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος εἰσαγαγόντα τοὺς πιστοὺς ὅπου ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη. Ἐκείνη Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν τὸν βότρυν ἐπὶ ξύλου ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐξαγαγόντα· οὗτος τὸν 1 ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν ὑπεδέξατο τὸν τὸν λῃστὴν εἰς τὸν παράδεισον εἰσαγαγόνταου διὰσλω 16 οι lacuna quinque linearumἩ πηγὴ τῆς Ἰεριχὼ ἦν πρότερον ἀγονίας μήτηρ, ἀκαρπίας τροφός, ἀτελὲς τὸ ὕδωρ ἔχουσα. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ῥεῖθρον ἀχανὲς εἶχεν, οἷον ἔλαιον ἀψοφητὶ ῥέουσα, ἡ δὲ τῶν ὑδάτων θέα διψῶν τας τοὺς θεωμένους ἀπέλυεν· οὐ γὰρ ἀκίνδυνος ἦν τοῖς δεομέ νοις ἡ πόσις· ὀλέθριον γὰρ εἶχε τὸ νᾶμα. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ κάλλος τῆς πηγῆς πρὸς δρόμον ἐκίνει τοὺς παριόντας, ὁ δὲ φόβος τῆς βλάβης τὴν προθυμίαν ἀνέκοπτεν.
thought_title: Nothing raises the soul like repentance; Zacchaeus as model
orientation: Amphilochius opens his homily to the congregation by praising repentance and then introduces Zacchaeus the chief tax collector of Jericho as the day's subject.
pass_a_gloss: In Zacchaeum. Of Amphilochius bishop of Iconium a discourse on Zacchaeus. Nothing so rouses the soul toward gladness as fear of God and abstinence from evils and the course of repentance and the manner of confession. Whence also today David blessed those who obtained the forgiveness of sins, at once presenting the love for humanity of Christ, and at once also preparing sinners to run to repentance ... Blessed, he says, are those whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered ... Let every fornicator and tax collector run to the inexhaustible springs of the salvation of Christ. It is not possible without it either to receive release from evils or to obtain the blessing, whether you speak of prophets or apostles or evangelists. For all drew from the same spring. Among prophets David himself, after adultery, still even now being a prophet through the grace of the one who forgave. Among apostles Peter and Paul, for the one after the denial holds the keys of the kingdom, and the other after the persecution was appointed apostle of the Gentiles, having changed the Jewish zeal into an evangelical manner. For in the gospels I know not only Matthew being saved from tax collectors, but also two others with him; of whom one, by praying, by striking the breast, the storehouse of evils, by not daring to lift the hands to the holy things, by looking down, not only was justified, but also was crowned over the Pharisee; and Zacchaeus, having gone up onto the tree on which often standing he watched lest any of the merchants pass by unnoticed so that he might not remain without profit, he watched lest the merchant of heaven and earth, the one carrying the inviolable treasury of the kingdom, run past him unnoticed. But lest we altogether confuse the stories of the tax collectors together, if it seems good, today taking Zacchaeus alone as the subject of our treatment let us broaden the discourse. Having gone out, it says, Jesus was passing through Jericho, and behold a man called by name Zacchaeus, and this man was a chief tax collector. Not simply does the evangelist mention Jericho, but because he says that a tax collector entertained God at home. And the matter was unbelievable. He sets forth his homeland, so that having remembered Rahab the prostitute we may not be startled at the strange recantation of Zacchaeus. For this reason therefore he mentioned Jericho, so that taking Rahab the prostitute into mind we may compare the manner of salvation of both. For just as Rahab the prostitute, having received Joshua son of Nun as a spy, hid him, so also Zacchaeus the tax collector, having received at home the true Jesus who spies out our mind, nourished him. She received Joshua son of Nun, the one who led the people into the land of promise; this man receives the true Jesus, the one who leads into the kingdom of the heavens. She received Joshua, the one who ... [lacuna of seven lines] ... this man received the true Jesus, the one who razed the temple of the Jews; For there shall not, he says, remain here a stone upon a stone which shall not be thrown down. She received Joshua, the one who through the Jordan led the people into a land flowing with milk and honey; this man received the true Jesus, the one who through baptism leads the faithful to where eye has not seen and ear has not heard and it has not gone up upon the heart of man. She received Joshua, the one who brought out the grape cluster on a tree from the land; this man received the true Jesus, the one who led the thief into paradise ... [lacuna of five lines] ... The spring of Jericho was formerly a mother of barrenness, a nurse of unfruitfulness, having imperfect water. For the stream had a broad current, flowing noiselessly like oil, but the sight of the waters sent away thirsty those who beheld them; for the drinking was not without danger to those in need; for the stream had a deadly flow. For the beauty of the spring moved those passing by to run, but the fear of harm cut short their eagerness.

choices.why: δρόμος means a running course or race; 'course' keeps the motion and the fixed path sense without over-polishing.

choices.english: the love for humanity of Christ
choices.why: Glossary requires 'love for humanity' for φιλανθρωπία; the genitive is kept literal.

choices.term: ἀκενώτους τῆς σωτηρίας τοῦ Χριστοῦ πηγάς
choices.english: the inexhaustible springs of the salvation of Christ
choices.why: πηγάς is plural and glossary gives 'spring'; 'inexhaustible' renders ἀκενώτους literally.
The phrase is appositional to the breast; literal rendering preserves the paradox of the breast as a storehouse of evils.
παλινῳδία means a formal retraction or reversal; 'recantation' captures the public turning-back sense.

choices.english: a mother of barrenness, a nurse of unfruitfulness
choices.why: The personifications are kept literal to preserve the rhetorical paradox of a spring that produces barrenness.
rejected: a source of sterility, a fosterer of unfruitfulness

pass_b_english: Nothing rouses the soul to gladness like the fear of God, turning away from evil, the course of repentance, and the way of confession. That is why David today blessed those who had received forgiveness of sins, showing at once Christ's love for humanity and preparing sinners to run to repentance. “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven,” he says, “and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1 LXX; Psalm 32:1 in the Hebrew numbering). So let every prostitute and tax collector run to the inexhaustible springs of Christ's salvation. Without it there is no release from evils and no attaining the blessing, whether you speak of prophets, apostles, or evangelists. For all drew from the same spring. Among the prophets, David himself, even after adultery, is still a prophet now through the grace of the One who forgave him. Among the apostles, Peter and Paul: the one, after his denial, holds the keys of the kingdom; the other, after his persecution, was appointed apostle to the Gentiles, turning his Jewish zeal into an evangelical way of life. In the Gospels I know not only Matthew being saved from among the tax collectors, but two others with him. One of them, by praying, by beating his breast—the treasury of evils—by not daring to raise his hands to the holy things, by bowing down, was not only justified but crowned above the Pharisee. Zacchaeus, for his part, climbed the tree where he had often stood watching to see whether some merchant might slip past unnoticed so that he would not go without profit; he was keeping watch so that the Merchant of heaven and earth, the One carrying the inviolable treasure of the kingdom, might not run past him unnoticed.

But so that we do not entirely confuse the stories of the tax collectors, let us, if you agree, take Zacchaeus alone today as the subject of our treatment and expand our discourse. “Jesus went out,” it says, “and was passing through Jericho, and behold, a man named Zacchaeus, and he was a chief tax collector” (Luke 19:1). The evangelist does not mention Jericho without purpose, but because he is speaking of a tax collector who welcomed God into his home. The matter was hard to believe. He sets his homeland before us, so that when we remember Rahab the prostitute we may not be shocked at the strange turning back of Zacchaeus. This is why he mentioned Jericho: so that, calling to mind Rahab the prostitute, we may compare the manner of salvation of both. For just as Rahab the prostitute received Joshua son of Nun as a spy and hid him, so Zacchaeus the tax collector received the true Jesus, who spies out our minds, into his home and nourished him. She received Joshua son of Nun, who led the people into the land of promise; this man receives the true Jesus, who leads into the kingdom of heaven. She received Joshua, who razed the temple of the Jews; this man received the true Jesus, who foretold that razing. For he says, “Not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be thrown down” (Matthew 24:2). She received Joshua, who led the people through the Jordan into a land flowing with milk and honey; this man received the true Jesus, who through baptism leads the faithful to what no eye has seen and no ear has heard and what has not entered the human heart (1 Corinthians 2:9). She received Joshua, who brought the cluster of grapes out of the land on a tree; this man welcomed the true Jesus, [lacuna] this man welcomed the true Jesus, who brought the thief into paradise.

The spring of Jericho was formerly a mother of barrenness, a nurse of unfruitfulness, its water incomplete. Its stream flowed silently, like oil flowing without a sound, but the sight of its waters left those who looked on thirsting. Drinking was not without danger for those in need, for its current was deadly. The beauty of the spring stirred passersby to run toward it, but the fear of harm cut short their eagerness.
notes: The source contains two lacunae: one of seven lines after 'Ἐκείνη Ἰησοῦν ἐδέξατο τὸν' and one of five lines after 'εἰσαγαγόνταου διὰσλω 16 οι'. The gloss marks these lacunae and does not supply missing text.

The phrase 'εἰσαγαγόνταου διὰσλω 16 οι' appears to be OCR damage or corruption immediately before the five-line lacuna; the gloss renders only the legible portion 'the one who led the thief into paradise' and notes the damage.

The phrase 'τις οὖνη πόρνοςτελώνης' appears to be OCR damage for 'πᾶς οὖν πόρνος καὶ τελώνης' or similar; the gloss renders 'every fornicator and tax collector' based on the legible elements and notes the uncertainty.
The phrase 'τὸν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶ κατ' is truncated in the source; the gloss renders 'the one who leads into the kingdom of the heavens' and notes the truncation.

problems.quote: the practice of confession
problems.why: ἐξομολόγησις here means public praise/acknowledgment of God's mercy, not sacramental confession.
problems.fix: the way of praise

problems.quote: so that he would not go unpenalized
problems.why: Zacchaeus wants to catch merchants to penalize/extract payment from them; 'go unpenalized' reverses agency.
problems.fix: so that they would not escape penalty
problems.ruling: ὅπως μὴ ἀζήμιος μείνῃ: Zacchaeus watches lest a merchant escape UNPENALIZED by him; 'go unpenalized' reverses agency.

problems.quote: who leads into the kingdom of heaven
problems.source_quote: τὸν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν κατ...
problems.why: Text breaks off with κατ- (probably κατάγοντα 'leading down'); 'leads into' assumes completion.
problems.fix: who leads down into the kingdom of heaven
problems.ruling: Source has lacuna after κατ-; translator supplies 'leads into' without noting the text breaks off, misleading the reader.

problems.quote: Psalm 31:1 LXX; 32:1 MT
problems.source_quote: μακάριοι, φησίν, ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι
problems.why: The citation is Psalm 31:2 LXX / 32:1 MT, not 31:1 LXX. The verse numbering is off by one in LXX.
problems.fix: Psalm 31:2 LXX; 32:1 MT
problems.ruling: LXX Psalm 31:2 (not 31:1) matches μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι; verse number is wrong.

problems.quote: so that they would not escape penalty
problems.why: ἀζήμιος means 'without loss/damage' to Zacchaeus himself, i.e., so he wouldn't miss his profit; not 'they would not escape penalty.'
problems.fix: so that he would not go without profit
problems.ruling: ἀζήμιος means 'without loss'; Zacchaeus feared missing his own profit, not that merchants escape penalty.

problems.quote: by looking down
problems.why: κάτω νεύειν means 'to bend down, bow down' (in humility), not 'looking down' which suggests looking downward with eyes; this reverses the physical and spiritual meaning.
problems.fix: by bowing down
problems.ruling: κάτω νεύειν means 'bowing down' in humility; 'looking down' misleads readers about the physical action.

problems.quote: the sight of its waters sent the thirsty away still thirsting
problems.source_quote: ἡ δὲ τῶν ὑδάτων θέα διψῶντας τοὺς θεωμένους ἀπέλυεν
problems.why: ἀπέλυεν means 'dismissed, sent away,' but the point is paradoxical: the sight of water made those who looked at it thirsty (the water was deceptive/unsatisfying); 'sent the thirsty away still thirsting' changes the meaning—the waters made them thirsty, they didn't just fail to satisfy existing thirst.
problems.fix: the sight of its waters left those who looked on thirsting
problems.ruling: θέα διψῶντας τοὺς θεωμένους ἀπέλυεν: the sight made viewers thirsty; English reverses cause and effect.

problems.quote: the strange recantation of Zacchaeus
problems.why: 'Recantation' means withdrawing a belief/statement; παλινοδία here means 'return/change of course' (repentance/turning back). Zacchaeus is not recanting doctrine but turning from sin.
problems.fix: the strange turning back of Zacchaeus
problems.ruling: παλινοδία means turning back/repentance, not 'recantation' (doctrinal renunciation); misleading for Zacchaeus's turning from sin.

problems.quote: Psalm 31:2 LXX; 32:1 MT
problems.source_quote: μακάριοι, φησίν, ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι
problems.why: The citation format is wrong. The source quotes Psalm 31:1-2 LXX (which is Psalm 32:1-2 MT). The English gives '31:2 LXX; 32:1 MT' but the quote begins with 'Blessed are those' which is verse 1 in both, and 'whose lawless deeds are forgiven' is verse 1 LXX/verse 1 MT. The numbering is garbled: should be Psalm 31:1 LXX / 32:1 MT, not 31:2.
problems.fix: Psalm 31:1 LXX; 32:1 MT
problems.ruling: Quote is μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν (Ps 31:1 LXX), not v.2; citation '31:2 LXX' is wrong verse number.

problems.quote: the strange recantation
problems.why: παλινοδία means 'return, turning back, recurrence'—here specifically repentance/return to God. 'Recantation' is a false friend suggesting doctrinal renunciation. The preacher means Zacchaeus's surprising repentance/turning from sin.
problems.fix: the strange turning back
problems.ruling: Duplicate of #1; παλινοδία means repentance/turning, 'recantation' misleads readers into thinking doctrinal renunciation.

edits.old: the true Jesus, who spies out our minds
edits.new: the true Jesus, who searches our hearts

fixed: The phrase 'the true Jesus' is correct and intentional: the source contrasts 'Ἰησοῦν τὸν τοῦ Ναυή' (Joshua son of Nun) with 'τὸν ἀληθινὸν Ἰησοῦν' (the true Jesus), so 'true Jesus' is the right rendering and should not be changed.

The source has 'τὸν κατασκοπεύοντα ἡμῶν τὴν διάνοιαν' (the one who spies out our mind). 'Spies out' is a literal rendering of κατασκοπεύω, but in English it carries a negative espionage connotation. The context is Christ's loving discernment of hearts, so 'searches our hearts' better conveys the sense while remaining faithful to the Greek.

The typological pairing of Joshua and Jesus is already clear in the English: the passage repeatedly contrasts 'Joshua son of Nun' with 'the true Jesus.' No additional note is needed in the translation itself.
